claim: Doc2a and Doc2b are high-affinity calcium-binding proteins that interact with SNARE proteins and phospholipids.
source: Doc2a and Doc2b are high-affinity calcium-binding proteins that interact with SNARE proteins and phospholipids.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the biochemical properties of Doc2 proteins, supported by the cited literature.

claim: Experiments performed on cultured cells indicated that Doc2 proteins promote spontaneous vesicle fusion and asynchronous neurotransmitter release.
source: Experiments performed on cultured cells indicated that Doc2 proteins promote spontaneous vesicle fusion and asynchronous neurotransmitter release, regulate vesicle priming, mediate augmentation, and regulate transmission during sustained activity.
evidence: This claim references previous experimental findings from cultured cell studies.

claim: Doc2 proteins regulate vesicle priming.
source: Experiments performed on cultured cells indicated that Doc2 proteins promote spontaneous vesicle fusion and asynchronous neurotransmitter release, regulate vesicle priming, mediate augmentation, and regulate transmission during sustained activity.
evidence: This claim references previous experimental findings from cultured cell studies.

claim: Doc2 proteins mediate augmentation.
source: Experiments performed on cultured cells indicated that Doc2 proteins promote spontaneous vesicle fusion and asynchronous neurotransmitter release, regulate vesicle priming, mediate augmentation, and regulate transmission during sustained activity.
evidence: This claim references previous experimental findings from cultured cell studies.

claim: Doc2 proteins regulate transmission during sustained activity.
source: Experiments performed on cultured cells indicated that Doc2 proteins promote spontaneous vesicle fusion and asynchronous neurotransmitter release, regulate vesicle priming, mediate augmentation, and regulate transmission during sustained activity.
evidence: This claim references previous experimental findings from cultured cell studies.

claim: PCs express Doc2b but not Doc2a.
source: PCs express Doc2b but not Doc2a.
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1A and cited literature (Verhage et al., 1997; Groffen et al., 2010).

claim: Spontaneous neurotransmitter release was normal in Doc2b KO mice at PC-to-DCN synapses.
source: Surprisingly, spontaneous neurotransmitter release, synaptic strength, the time course of evoked release, responses evoked by sustained high-frequency stimulation, and short-term plasticity were normal in Doc2b KO mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E-F comparing mIPSC frequency between WT and Doc2b KO.

claim: Synaptic strength was normal in Doc2b KO mice at PC-to-DCN synapses.
source: Surprisingly, spontaneous neurotransmitter release, synaptic strength, the time course of evoked release, responses evoked by sustained high-frequency stimulation, and short-term plasticity were normal in Doc2b KO mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 comparing single fiber conductances between WT and Doc2b KO.

claim: The time course of evoked release was normal in Doc2b KO mice at PC-to-DCN synapses.
source: Surprisingly, spontaneous neurotransmitter release, synaptic strength, the time course of evoked release, responses evoked by sustained high-frequency stimulation, and short-term plasticity were normal in Doc2b KO mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-C comparing IPSC decay time constants between WT and Doc2b KO.

claim: Responses evoked by sustained high-frequency stimulation were normal in Doc2b KO mice at PC-to-DCN synapses.
source: Surprisingly, spontaneous neurotransmitter release, synaptic strength, the time course of evoked release, responses evoked by sustained high-frequency stimulation, and short-term plasticity were normal in Doc2b KO mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4 comparing responses during sustained stimulation between WT and Doc2b KO.

claim: Short-term plasticity was normal in Doc2b KO mice at PC-to-DCN synapses.
source: Surprisingly, spontaneous neurotransmitter release, synaptic strength, the time course of evoked release, responses evoked by sustained high-frequency stimulation, and short-term plasticity were normal in Doc2b KO mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4 comparing paired pulse ratios and facilitation between WT and Doc2b KO.

claim: Doc2b removal does not influence transmission at PC-to-DCN synapses under physiological conditions.
source: Thus, in stark contrast to numerous functions previously proposed for Doc2, here we find that Doc2b removal does not influence transmission at PC-to-DCN synapses, indicating that conclusions based on studies of Doc2b in cultured cells do not necessarily generalize to mature synapses under physiological conditions.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Conclusions based on studies of Doc2b in cultured cells do not necessarily generalize to mature synapses under physiological conditions.
source: Thus, in stark contrast to numerous functions previously proposed for Doc2, here we find that Doc2b removal does not influence transmission at PC-to-DCN synapses, indicating that conclusions based on studies of Doc2b in cultured cells do not necessarily generalize to mature synapses under physiological conditions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the contrast between previous cultured cell studies and the current findings at mature synapses.

claim: Syt1 and Syt2 bind calcium with low affinity and fast kinetics to mediate fast synaptic transmission.
source: Some of these proteins (Syt1 and Syt2) bind calcium with low affinity and fast kinetics to mediate fast synaptic transmission (Fernández-Chacón et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Synaptotagmin proteins, supported by the cited reference.

claim: Syt7 binds Ca with high affinity and slow kinetics and mediates facilitation and asynchronous neurotransmitter release.
source: Others, such as Syt7, bind Ca with high affinity and slow kinetics and mediate facilitation and asynchronous neurotransmitter release (Wen et al., 2010; Jackman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Syt7, supported by the cited references.

claim: Doc2b and Doc2a bind calcium with high affinity.
source: Doc2b and Doc2a also bind calcium with high affinity, but their contribution to synaptic transmission is unclear.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Doc2 proteins' biochemical properties.

claim: The contribution of Doc2b and Doc2a to synaptic transmission is unclear.
source: Doc2b and Doc2a also bind calcium with high affinity, but their contribution to synaptic transmission is unclear.
evidence: This statement reflects the uncertainty in the field that motivates the current study.

claim: Doc2b and Doc2a function in a similar manner but can be differentially expressed.
source: These proteins are understood to function in a similar manner but can be differentially expressed (Courtney et al., 2018; Verhage et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Doc2 proteins, supported by the cited references.

claim: In hippocampal cultures, Doc2b knockout reduced the frequency of miniature postsynaptic currents compared to control.
source: In hippocampal cultures, Doc2b knockout (KO) reduced the frequency of miniature postsynaptic currents ('minis') compared to control (Groffen et al., 2010; Courtney et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies, supported by the cited references.

claim: Reduction in mini frequency has been observed at Purkinje cell to PC collateral synapses in acute slices from P7-8 Doc2b KO mice.
source: This reduction in mini frequency has also been observed at Purkinje cell (PC) to PC collateral synapses in acute slices from P7-8 Doc2b KO mice (Groffen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study, supported by the cited reference.

claim: Doc2b has been proposed to be a Ca sensor for spontaneous release.
source: These results led to the proposal that Doc2b is a Ca sensor for spontaneous release.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous studies, based on the cited findings.

claim: Doc2b and Doc2a have been proposed to be Ca sensors for asynchronous release in hippocampal cultures.
source: Doc2b and Doc2a have also been proposed to be Ca sensors for asynchronous release in hippocampal cultures (Yao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from a previous study, supported by the cited reference.

claim: Doc2 proteins have been reported to mediate synaptic augmentation in hippocampal cultures.
source: Another study from hippocampal cultures reported that Doc2 proteins mediate synaptic augmentation (Xue et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study, supported by the cited reference.

claim: In cultured chromaffin cells, Doc2b is thought to act as a Ca sensor for vesicle priming.
source: Furthermore, in cultured chromaffin cells, Doc2b is thought to act as a Ca sensor for vesicle priming (Houy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from a previous study, supported by the cited reference.

claim: The role of Doc2b at mature synapses under physiological conditions remains unaddressed.
source: Despite the intriguing results of these studies, the role of Doc2b at mature synapses under physiological conditions remains unaddressed.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature that motivates the current study.

claim: PCs form powerful synapses onto neurons in the DCN which relay cerebellar output to numerous brain regions.
source: PCs form powerful synapses onto neurons in the DCN which relay cerebellar output to numerous brain regions.
evidence: This is established anatomical and functional knowledge about cerebellar circuitry.

claim: Doc2b is expressed in PCs but Doc2a is not.
source: This synapse was chosen because Doc2b is expressed in PCs but Doc2a is not (Verhage et al., 1997; Groffen et al., 2010), and because Doc2b might contribute to several distinguishing features of this synapse.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and confirmed by FISH data in Figure 1.

claim: The PC to DCN synapse remains effective even for high-frequency sustained activation, as is typical in vivo.
source: The PC to DCN synapse remains effective even for high-frequency sustained activation, as is typical in vivo (Turecek et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the PC to DCN synapse, supported by the cited references.

claim: A specialized vesicle pool with a very low initial probability of release is thought to mediate transmission during high-frequency activation at the PC to DCN synapse.
source: Furthermore, a specialized vesicle pool with a very low initial probability of release is thought to mediate transmission during high-frequency activation, but this pool is poorly understood.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the PC to DCN synapse based on previous studies.

claim: Facilitation at the PC to DCN synapse helps these synapses maintain frequency-invariance.
source: Second, facilitation at the PC to DCN synapse helps these synapses maintain frequency-invariance (Turecek et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the PC to DCN synapse, supported by the cited reference.

claim: Syt7 has been proposed to mediate facilitation at the PC to DCN synapse.
source: Although Syt7 has been proposed to mediate facilitation at the PC to DCN synapse, we tested the possibility that Doc2b also contributes to short-term synaptic plasticity and frequency-invariance.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous studies about the role of Syt7.

claim: No aspect of PC to DCN transmission was altered in Doc2b KO mice.
source: Unexpectedly, no aspect of PC to DCN transmission was altered in Doc2b KO mice.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figures 1-4.

claim: PCs strongly expressed Doc2b but not Doc2a in wildtype animals.
source: PCs strongly expressed Doc2b but not Doc2a in wildtype animals (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In PCs of Doc2b KO mice, Doc2b expression was eliminated and Doc2a expression remained absent.
source: In PCs of Doc2b KO mice, Doc2b expression was eliminated and Doc2a expression remained absent (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In wildtype animals, DCN neurons did not express either Doc2b or Doc2a.
source: In wildtype animals, DCN neurons did not express either Doc2b or Doc2a (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Doc2b was apparent in the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus of wildtype animals but was absent in the KO.
source: Doc2b was apparent in the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus (Verhage et al., 1997; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and the striatum (data not shown) of wildtype animals but was absent in the KO (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Doc2b was apparent in the striatum of wildtype animals but was absent in the KO.
source: Doc2b was apparent in the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus (Verhage et al., 1997; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and the striatum (data not shown) of wildtype animals but was absent in the KO (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text but data are not shown.

claim: Doc2a expression was apparent in the CA3 region of the hippocampus in both WT and Doc2b KO.
source: Doc2a expression was apparent in the CA3 region of the hippocampus in both WT and Doc2b KO (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Doc2b protein colocalizes with parvalbumin, a marker for PC boutons, in the DCN of WT animals.
source: Furthermore, we used immunostaining to demonstrate that Doc2b protein colocalizes with parvalbumin, a marker for PC boutons, in the DCN of WT animals (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Doc2b immunoreactivity was not detected in Doc2b KO animals.
source: Doc2b immunoreactivity was not detected in Doc2b KO animals (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Doc2b immunoreactivity was prominent in PC cell bodies and dendrites and in other brain regions including the hippocampus.
source: Doc2b immunoreactivity was also prominent in PC cell bodies and dendrites and in other brain regions including the hippocampus (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Doc2b is the only calcium-dependent Doc2 present at PC synapses of adult wildtype mice.
source: These studies indicate that Doc2b is the only calcium-dependent Doc2 present at PC synapses of adult wildtype mice, that it is eliminated in Doc2b KO mice, and that there is no compensatory expression of Doc2a in PCs of Doc2b KO mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FISH and immunostaining data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Doc2b is eliminated in Doc2b KO mice.
source: These studies indicate that Doc2b is the only calcium-dependent Doc2 present at PC synapses of adult wildtype mice, that it is eliminated in Doc2b KO mice, and that there is no compensatory expression of Doc2a in PCs of Doc2b KO mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FISH and immunostaining data presented in Figure 1.

claim: There is no compensatory expression of Doc2a in PCs of Doc2b KO mice.
source: These studies indicate that Doc2b is the only calcium-dependent Doc2 present at PC synapses of adult wildtype mice, that it is eliminated in Doc2b KO mice, and that there is no compensatory expression of Doc2a in PCs of Doc2b KO mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FISH data presented in Figure 1.

claim: There was no difference in mIPSC frequency for WT and Doc2b KO mice at the mature PC to DCN synapse under physiological conditions (p=0.93).
source: Surprisingly, however, there was no difference in mIPSC frequency for WT and Doc2b KO mice at the mature PC to DCN synapse under physiological conditions (34-35o C, 1.5 mM external calcium, Cae) (p=0.93, two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test) (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E-F with statistical analysis.

claim: Doc2b KO causes a strong reduction in mIPSC frequency in hippocampal autapse cultures.
source: This contrasts with the strong reduction in mIPSC frequency that Doc2b KO causes in hippocampal autapse cultures (Groffen et al., 2010), hippocampal neuronal cultures (Courtney et al., 2018; Groffen et al., 2010; Pang et al., 2011; Ramirez et al., 2017), and PC to PC synapses (Groffen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies, supported by the cited references.

claim: Doc2b KO causes a strong reduction in mIPSC frequency in hippocampal neuronal cultures.
source: This contrasts with the strong reduction in mIPSC frequency that Doc2b KO causes in hippocampal autapse cultures (Groffen et al., 2010), hippocampal neuronal cultures (Courtney et al., 2018; Groffen et al., 2010; Pang et al., 2011; Ramirez et al., 2017), and PC to PC synapses (Groffen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies, supported by the cited references.

claim: Doc2b KO causes a 75% reduction in mIPSC frequency at PC to PC synapses.
source: In the latter case, the observed 75% reduction in mIPSC frequency at PC to PC synapses is paricularly interesting because it also involves synapses made by PCs.
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study (Groffen et al., 2010).

claim: Experiments at PC to PC synapses were performed in brain slices of P7-P8 mice at room temperature in elevated Cae (2.0 mM).
source: In contrast to our PC to DCN studies which were perfomed in near physiological conditions (34-35o C, 1.5 Cae), experiments at PC to PC synapses were performed in brain slices of P7-P8 mice at room temperature in elevated Cae (2.0 mM).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions used in previous studies.

claim: mIPSC frequency was reduced by 65% in P7-P8 Doc2b KO mice for experiments performed at 34-35°C and in 1.5 Cae (p<0.001).
source: We found that mIPSC frequency was reduced by 65% in P7-P8 in Doc2b KO mice for experiments that were performed at 34-35o C and in 1.5 Cae (p<0.001, two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 with statistical analysis.

claim: The age of the animal could account for the Doc2b dependence of mIPSC frequency.
source: This result suggests that the age of the animal could account for the Doc2b dependence of mIPSC frequency.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing results at different ages.

claim: PCs are the dominant source of inhibition for other PCs for only a brief developmental window.
source: It is impractical to extend studies of the PC to PC synapse to older animals because PCs are the dominant source of inhibition for other PCs for only a brief developmental window, and in older animals, molecular layer interneurons become the dominant source of inhibition (Altman, 1972; Bernard and Axelrad, 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar development, supported by the cited references.

claim: In older animals, molecular layer interneurons become the dominant source of inhibition onto PCs.
source: It is impractical to extend studies of the PC to PC synapse to older animals because PCs are the dominant source of inhibition for other PCs for only a brief developmental window, and in older animals, molecular layer interneurons become the dominant source of inhibition (Altman, 1972; Bernard and Axelrad, 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar development, supported by the cited references.

claim: Doc2b contributes to mini release in developing animals but not in adults.
source: These observations suggest that Doc2b contributes to mini release in developing animals but not in adults.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing results at different ages.

claim: There was no difference in mini release in Doc2b KO mice at the PC to DCN synapse in P11-12 animals (p=0.57).
source: To address this possibility, we repeated experiments at the PC to DCN synapse in P11-12 animals, but again observed no difference in mini release in Doc2b KO mice (p=0.57, two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test) (Figure 1G–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G-H with statistical analysis.

claim: Doc2b is present both presynaptically and postsynaptically at PC to PC synapses and at many cultured synapses.
source: Another potential issue in interpreting previous studies is that Doc2b is present both presynaptically and postsynaptically at PC to PC synapses and at many cultured synapses that have been studied.
evidence: This is an observation about the expression pattern of Doc2b.

claim: Doc2b is thought to function presynaptically.
source: Although Doc2b is thought to function presynaptically, it remains possible that Doc2b may act postsynaptically to influence mini frequency.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous studies.

claim: At the parallel fiber to PC synapse, Doc2b is normally expressed in the postsynaptic PC, but not in the presynaptic granule cells.
source: We therefore tested whether postsynaptic loss of Doc2b affects mini frequency by recording miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) at the parallel fiber to PC synapse, in which Doc2b is normally expressed in the postsynaptic PC, but not in the presynaptic granule cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At the parallel fiber to PC synapse, there was no effect on mEPSC frequency or amplitudes in Doc2b KO mice (p=0.83).
source: At the parallel fiber to PC synapse, we saw no effect on mEPSC frequency or amplitudes in Doc2b KO mice (p=0.83), arguing against a postsynaptic contribution of Doc2b to minis (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 with statistical analysis.

claim: There is no postsynaptic contribution of Doc2b to minis.
source: At the parallel fiber to PC synapse, we saw no effect on mEPSC frequency or amplitudes in Doc2b KO mice (p=0.83), arguing against a postsynaptic contribution of Doc2b to minis (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mEPSC data at the parallel fiber to PC synapse.

claim: The peak single fiber conductances were similar for WT and Doc2b KO mice (p=0.22).
source: The peak single fiber conductances were similar for WT and Doc2b KO mice (p=0.22, two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test) (WT: 30.9 ± 3.5 nS, n = 30 inputs, Doc2b KO: 26.9 ± 2.7, n = 29 inputs), indicating that the loss of Doc2b does not alter evoked release at the PC to DCN synapse.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 with statistical analysis.

claim: The loss of Doc2b does not alter evoked release at the PC to DCN synapse.
source: The peak single fiber conductances were similar for WT and Doc2b KO mice (p=0.22, two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test) (WT: 30.9 ± 3.5 nS, n = 30 inputs, Doc2b KO: 26.9 ± 2.7, n = 29 inputs), indicating that the loss of Doc2b does not alter evoked release at the PC to DCN synapse.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the single fiber conductance data.

claim: The high affinity and slow kinetics of calcium-binding made Doc2 a strong candidate sensor for asynchronous release.
source: The high affinity and slow kinetics of calcium-binding made Doc2 a strong candidate sensor for asynchronous release, and a study concluded that Doc2 mediates slow asynchronous release in hippocampal cultures (Yao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the biochemical properties of Doc2 and previous studies.

claim: A study concluded that Doc2 mediates slow asynchronous release in hippocampal cultures.
source: The high affinity and slow kinetics of calcium-binding made Doc2 a strong candidate sensor for asynchronous release, and a study concluded that Doc2 mediates slow asynchronous release in hippocampal cultures (Yao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study, supported by the cited reference.

claim: The decays of the synaptic currents were unaltered in Doc2b KO mice.
source: However, we found that the decays of the synaptic currents were unaltered in Doc2b KO mice (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: The IPSC decay time constants were similar for WT and Doc2b KO mice (p=0.45).
source: The IPSC decay time constants were similar for WT and Doc2b KO mice (p=0.45, two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test) (WT: 3.43 ± 0.18 ms, Doc2b KO: 3.63 ± 0.17 ms).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C with statistical analysis.

claim: There was a high frequency (50–100 Hz) of spontaneous IPSCs onto DCN cells.
source: There was a high frequency (50–100 Hz) of spontaneous IPSCs onto DCN cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental recordings.

claim: During failure trials, there was no change in spontaneous event frequency.
source: As expected, during failure trials, there was no change in spontaneous event frequency (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a transient decrease in sIPSC frequency after a success trial.
source: Instead there was a transient decrease in sIPSC frequency.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The transient decrease in sIPSC frequency was present in both WT and Doc2b KO mice.
source: This reduction was present in both WT and Doc2b KO mice and could be lengthened by stimulating PCs 4 times at 100 Hz (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Asynchronous release is not detected at the PC to DCN synapse in WT or Doc2b KO animals.
source: However, with regard to the issue of asynchronous release, these experiments demonstrate that asynchronous release is not detected at the PC to DCN synapse in WT or Doc2b KO animals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of spontaneous events after stimulation.

claim: PCs usually fire at high frequencies for sustained periods.
source: PCs usually fire at high frequencies for sustained periods, and it is therefore important to use appropriate stimulus patterns to assess the contribution of Doc2b under physiological conditions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PC firing patterns in vivo.

claim: The PC to DCN synapse changes considerably during development.
source: The PC to DCN synapse changes considerably during development.
evidence: This is established knowledge about synaptic development.

claim: At the PC to DCN synapse in juveniles, synaptic depression is prominent and becomes more pronounced at higher PC stimulation frequencies.
source: We began by studying the PC to DCN synapse in juveniles, where synaptic depression is prominent and becomes more pronounced at higher PC stimulation frequencies (Figure 3; Turecek et al., 2017; Turecek et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and cited literature.

claim: In both WT and Doc2b KO mice, frequency-dependent synaptic depression was readily observable at juvenile PC to DCN synapses.
source: In both WT and Doc2b KO mice, frequency-dependent synaptic depression was readily observable, and responses from individual cells were comparable (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Paired pulse plasticity was unaffected by the loss of Doc2b (p=0.74).
source: Paired pulse plasticity was unaffected by the loss of Doc2b (p=0.74, two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test) (Figure 3C), suggesting that Doc2b does not contribute to the initial probability of release.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C with statistical analysis.

claim: Doc2b does not contribute to the initial probability of release at the PC to DCN synapse.
source: Paired pulse plasticity was unaffected by the loss of Doc2b (p=0.74, two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test) (Figure 3C), suggesting that Doc2b does not contribute to the initial probability of release.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the paired pulse plasticity data.

claim: There was no difference in the magnitude of the steady-state IPSCs between WT and Doc2b KO (p=0.64).
source: We found no difference in the magnitude of the steady-state IPSCs between WT and Doc2b KO (p=0.64) (Figure 3D), and the kinetics of reaching steady-state were unaltered in Doc2b KO mice (p=0.83) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D with statistical analysis.

claim: The kinetics of reaching steady-state were unaltered in Doc2b KO mice (p=0.83).
source: We found no difference in the magnitude of the steady-state IPSCs between WT and Doc2b KO (p=0.64) (Figure 3D), and the kinetics of reaching steady-state were unaltered in Doc2b KO mice (p=0.83) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E with statistical analysis.

claim: Doc2b does not play a role in synaptic transmission during ongoing activity in juvenile PC to DCN synapses.
source: These results demonstrate that Doc2b does not play a role in synaptic transmission during ongoing activity in juvenile PC to DCN synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: In adults, steady-state transmission at PC to DCN synapses is frequency-independent.
source: In adults, steady-state transmission at PC to DCN synapses is frequency-independent (Turecek et al., 2017; Turecek et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about adult PC to DCN synapses, supported by the cited references.

claim: Frequency-invariance at PC to DCN synapses requires a precise balance between activity-dependent vesicle depletion and activity-dependent facilitation mediated by Syt7.
source: This unusual property requires a precise balance between activity-dependent vesicle depletion and activity-dependent facilitation mediated by Syt7 (Turecek et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of frequency-invariance, supported by the cited reference.

claim: Synaptic responses are present during sustained high-frequency activation in Syt7 KO mice, although they are no longer frequency-invariant.
source: However, synaptic responses are present during sustained high-frequency activation in Syt7 KO mice, although they are no longer frequency-invariant (Turecek et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study, supported by the cited reference.

claim: There must be Syt7-independent mechanisms that help sustain release after repetitive PC activity.
source: Therefore, there must be Syt7-independent mechanisms that help sustain release after repetitive PC activity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that synaptic responses persist in Syt7 KO mice.

claim: Frequency-invariance is readily observed at the PC to DCN synapse in adult WT mice.
source: Frequency-invariance is readily observed at this age in WT, as steady-state synaptic strength remains constant across PC firing frequency (Figure 4A; Turecek et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and cited literature.

claim: In Doc2b KO mice, there was no difference in synaptic responses compared to WT mice at adult PC to DCN synapses, and frequency-invariance remained intact.
source: In Doc2b KO mice, we observed no difference in synaptic responses compared to WT mice, and frequency-invariance remained intact (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Steady-state synaptic strength was normal in Doc2b KO at adult PC to DCN synapses (p=0.32).
source: Specifically, steady-state synaptic strength and the kinetics of reaching steady-state were normal in Doc2b KO (p=0.32 and p=0.51, respectively) (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C with statistical analysis.

claim: The kinetics of reaching steady-state were normal in Doc2b KO at adult PC to DCN synapses (p=0.51).
source: Specifically, steady-state synaptic strength and the kinetics of reaching steady-state were normal in Doc2b KO (p=0.32 and p=0.51, respectively) (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D with statistical analysis.

claim: There was no difference in the magnitude or time-course of facilitation in Doc2b KO at the PC to DCN synapse.
source: However, we did not observe any difference in the magnitude or time-course of facilitation in Doc2b KO at the PC to DCN synapse (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G-H.

claim: Doc2b does not contribute to PC to DCN synaptic transmission or short-term plasticity in young or mature animals under physiological conditions.
source: Altogether, our data do not support a role for Doc2b in PC to DCN synaptic transmission or short-term plasticity in young or mature animals under physiological conditions.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all the experimental data presented.

claim: The frequency of spontaneous release was unaltered in Doc2b KO mice, indicating that Doc2b is not a calcium sensor for spontaneous release at the PC to DCN synapse.
source: The frequency of spontaneous release was unaltered in Doc2b KO mice, indicating that Doc2b is not a calcium sensor for spontaneous release at this synapse (Courtney et al., 2018; Groffen et al., 2010; Pang et al., 2011; Ramirez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mIPSC frequency data, contrasting with previous studies.

claim: The PC to DCN synapse is extremely fast (average Tau decay = 2.1 ms).
